Chapter Three
第三章
There was music from my neighbour’s house through the summer nights.
一个个夏夜，隔壁那座宅子里总有音乐传来。
In his blue gardens men and girls came and went like moths among the whisperings and the champagne and the stars.
在那泛着蓝意的花园里，男人和姑娘们如飞蛾般往来，穿梭在私语、香槟与星光之间。
At high tide in the afternoon I watched his guests diving from the tower of his raft,
下午涨潮时，我看着他的客人从浮台上的跳水塔一头扎进水中，
or taking the sun on the hot sand of his beach while his two motorboats slit the waters of the Sound,
或者躺在他那片滚烫的沙滩上晒太阳。他的两艘汽艇从海峡水面上劈浪而过，
drawing aquaplanes over cataracts of foam.
拖着滑水板，越过瀑布似的层层白沫。
On weekends his Rolls-Royce became an omnibus, bearing parties to and from the city between nine in the morning
一到周末，他的劳斯莱斯就成了公共汽车，一拨拨地接送客人往返纽约城，从早上九点
and long past midnight, while his station wagon scampered like a brisk yellow bug to meet all trains.
一直接到午夜过了许久。他那辆旅行车则像只灵活的黄甲虫，每趟火车都赶去接。
And on Mondays eight servants, including an extra gardener, toiled all day with mops
每逢星期一，八个仆人（其中一个是额外请来的园丁）便抄起拖把、
and scrubbing-brushes and hammers and garden-shears, repairing the ravages of the night before.
硬毛刷、锤子和花剪，忙碌一整天，收拾前一夜留下的满目狼藉。
Every Friday five crates of oranges and lemons arrived from a fruiterer in New York—
每个星期五，纽约的水果商都会送来五箱橙子和柠檬；
every Monday these same oranges and lemons left his back door in a pyramid of pulpless halves.
到了星期一，这些水果就从后门运出去，只剩一座小山似的空壳，全都对半切开，挖空了果肉。
There was a machine in the kitchen
厨房里有一台机器，
which could extract the juice of two hundred oranges in half an hour if a little button was pressed two hundred times by a butler’s thumb.
半小时能榨两百个橙子，只消管家的拇指把一个小按钮按上两百次。
At least once a fortnight a corps of caterers came down with several hundred feet of canvas
每隔两周，至少有一回，一大队承办酒席的人会赶来，带着几百英尺长的帆布
and enough coloured lights to make a Christmas tree of Gatsby’s enormous garden.
和彩灯，那些灯足够把盖茨比的整座大花园装扮成一棵圣诞树。
On buffet tables, garnished with glistening hors-d’oeuvre, spiced baked hams crowded against salads of harlequin designs and pastry pigs and turkeys bewitched to a dark gold.
自助餐桌上缀着亮晶晶的开胃小菜；加了香料的烤火腿挤着五彩斑斓的沙拉、酥皮小猪，还有如施了魔法般泛着深金色的烤火鸡。
In the main hall a bar with a real brass rail was set up, and stocked with gins
正厅里架起一道酒吧，配着货真价实的黄铜栏杆，摆满了杜松子酒、
and liquors and with cordials so long forgotten that most of his female guests were too young to know one from another.
各种烈酒，还有些早已被人忘却的甜酒。女客们大多年纪太轻，连哪一种是哪一种都分不清。
By seven o’clock the orchestra has arrived, no thin five-piece affair, but a whole pitful of oboes
到了七点，乐队已经来了。可不是单薄的五人班子，来的阵势足足能坐满一个乐池：双簧管、
and trombones and saxophones and viols and cornets and piccolos, and low and high drums.
长号、萨克斯管、古提琴、短号、短笛，还有高低音的鼓，应有尽有。
The last swimmers have come in from the beach now and are dressing upstairs;
最后几个游泳的人也从沙滩回来了，正在楼上更衣。
the cars from New York are parked five deep in the drive, and already the halls
纽约城里来的汽车沿车道密密停了五层。大厅、
and salons and verandas are gaudy with primary colours, and hair bobbed in strange new ways, and shawls beyond the dreams of Castile.
会客室和敞廊里，到处是耀眼的红黄蓝，是式样新奇的短发，还有连卡斯蒂利亚人都梦不到的华丽披肩。
The bar is in full swing, and floating rounds of cocktails permeate the garden outside,
酒吧里正忙得热火朝天。一轮又一轮鸡尾酒游走在外面的花园里，
until the air is alive with chatter and laughter, and casual innuendo
四下沸腾着说笑声，夹杂着随口的暗示、
and introductions forgotten on the spot, and enthusiastic meetings between women who never knew each other’s names.
转眼就忘的人名介绍，还有些女人连对方叫什么都不知道，一见面却亲热得不得了。
The lights grow brighter as the earth lurches away from the sun,
大地摇摇晃晃地转离太阳，灯光愈来愈亮。
and now the orchestra is playing yellow cocktail music, and the opera of voices pitches a key higher.
乐队奏起了金黄色的鸡尾酒舞曲，人声汇成的一出歌剧也随之升高了一个调门。
Laughter is easier minute by minute, spilled with prodigality, tipped out at a cheerful word.
一分一秒过去，笑声越来越容易出口，任意倾洒；一句逗趣的话，便能倒出一串笑来。
The groups change more swiftly, swell with new arrivals, dissolve and form in the same breath;
人群变换得更快了，新客人来了，小圈子就胀大，一转眼又散开，重新聚拢。
already there are wanderers, confident girls who weave here and there among the stouter and more stable,
已有些人开始四处游走：自信满满的姑娘在较为富态、稳重的客人间穿梭，
become for a sharp, joyous moment the centre of a group, and then, excited with triumph,
一刹那间，便快快乐乐地成了某个圈子的中心。得意之余，她们兴致勃勃，
glide on through the sea-change of faces and voices and colour under the constantly changing light.
又轻盈地滑进那片人脸、声浪和色彩的流变之中，上方的灯光也在不停变幻。
Suddenly one of these gypsies, in trembling opal, seizes a cocktail out of the air,
忽然，其中一个吉卜赛女郎似的姑娘，浑身闪着欧泊般颤动的光彩，凌空抓过一杯鸡尾酒，
dumps it down for courage and, moving her hands like Frisco, dances out alone on the canvas platform.
一口灌下去壮胆。她学着弗里斯科的手势，独自跳上了铺着帆布的舞台。
A momentary hush; the orchestra leader varies his rhythm obligingly for her,
短暂的寂静；管弦乐队的指挥为她调整了节奏，
and there is a burst of chatter as the erroneous news goes around that she is Gilda Gray’s understudy from the Follies.
当这个错误消息传开时，人们开始议论纷纷，说她其实是吉尔达·格雷在Follies剧团的替补演员。
The party has begun.
派对已经开始了。
I believe that on the first night I went to Gatsby’s house I was one of the few guests who had actually been invited.
我认为，在我去盖茨比家的第一个晚上，我是少数几位真正被邀请的客人之一。
People were not invited—they went there.
人们并没有被邀请，他们就是去了那里。
They got into automobiles which bore them out to Long Island, and somehow they ended up at Gatsby’s door.
他们乘坐汽车前往长岛，最终来到了盖茨比的门前。
Once there they were introduced by somebody who knew Gatsby, and after
他们一到那里后，是由一位认识盖茨比的人为他们引荐的。
that they conducted themselves according to the rules of behaviour associated with an amusement park.
他们的行为举止都遵循着与游乐园相关的礼仪规范。
Sometimes they came and went without having met Gatsby at all,
有时候，他们来到这里，甚至没有遇到盖茨比，就离开了。
came for the party with a simplicity of heart that was its own ticket of admission.
他们来参加派对时，带着一种纯粹而简单的心情，这种心情本身就是他们进入派对的凭证。
I had been actually invited.
实际上，我确实被邀请了。
A chauffeur in a uniform of robin’s-egg blue crossed my lawn early
一位穿着罗宾蛋蓝色制服的司机很早就来到了我的草坪旁。
that Saturday morning with a surprisingly formal note from his employer:
那个星期六的早晨，尽管雇主要求他保持非常正式的着装——穿着罗宾蛋蓝色的制服。
the honour would be entirely Gatsby’s, it said, if I would attend his “little party” that night.
据说，如果我在那个晚上参加他的“小派对”，那么这份荣誉就完全属于盖茨比了。
He had seen me several times, and had intended to call on me long before,
他多次见过我，早在很久以前就打算去拜访我了。
but a peculiar combination of circumstances had prevented it—signed Jay Gatsby, in a majestic hand.
但某些特殊的情况阻碍了这一愿望的实现——署名是杰伊·盖茨比，用了一笔庄严的笔迹。
Dressed up in white flannels I went over to his lawn a little after seven,
穿着白色的法兰绒衣服，我七点刚过就走到他的草坪旁边，
and wandered around rather ill at ease among swirls and eddies of people I didn’t know—
我在那些我不认识的人中间，有些不安地四处走动——
though here and there was a face I had noticed on the commuting train.
虽然到处都有我在通勤列车上注意到的面孔。
I was immediately struck by the number of young Englishmen dotted about; all well dressed,
我立刻被那些在火车上四处游荡的年轻英国男子们所吸引；他们个个衣着整洁，看起来都很精明能干。
all looking a little hungry, and all talking in low, earnest voices to solid and prosperous Americans.
他们看起来都有些饥肠辘辘，都用低沉而专注的声音与那些富裕的美国人交谈着。
I was sure that they were selling something: bonds or insurance or automobiles.
我确信他们正在出售某种商品：债券、保险或汽车。
They were at least agonizingly aware of the easy money in the vicinity
他们至少清楚地意识到，周围那些轻松赚来的钱……
and convinced that it was theirs for a few words in the right key.
认准了只要几句话说得对路，那钱就能落进自己口袋。
As soon as I arrived I made an attempt to find my host,
我一到那里，就立刻尝试去找到我的主人。
but the two or three people of whom I asked his whereabouts stared at me in such an amazed way,
不过，那两三个问我他下落的人，都用一种惊讶的眼神盯着我。
and denied so vehemently any knowledge of his movements, that I slunk off in the direction of the cocktail table—
他坚决否认自己了解他的行踪，于是我悄悄地朝鸡尾酒桌的方向走去——
the only place in the garden where a single man could linger without looking purposeless and alone.
在花园里，只有这个地方可以让一个单身男子独自待着，而不会显得无目的或孤独。
I was on my way to get roaring drunk from sheer embarrassment when Jordan Baker came out of the house
当时我正准备因为尴尬而喝得酩酊，突然乔丹贝克从房子里出来
and stood at the head of the marble steps, leaning a little backward and looking with contemptuous interest down into the garden.
她站在大理石台阶的顶端，微微向后仰着身子，以轻蔑的兴致俯视着花园里的一切。
Welcome or not, I found it necessary to attach myself to someone before I should begin to address cordial remarks to the passersby.
无论是否受欢迎，我觉得在开始对路过的行人表示友善的问候之前，先与某个人建立联系是必要的。
“Hello!”
“你好！”
I roared, advancing toward her.
我大声吼叫着，向她冲去。
My voice seemed unnaturally loud across the garden.
我的声音在花园里显得异常响亮。
“I thought you might be here,” she responded absently as I came up.
“我以为你可能会在这里，”当我走近时，她心不在焉地回答道。
“I remembered you lived next door to—”
“我记得你住在隔壁……”
She held my hand impersonally, as a promise that she’d take care of me in a minute,
她以一种漠不关心的态度握着我的手，仿佛在承诺，她会立刻照顾我。
and gave ear to two girls in twin yellow dresses, who stopped at the foot of the steps.
她转而去听两个姑娘说话。她们穿着一模一样的黄裙子，在台阶脚下停了下来。
“Hello!” they cried together.
“你好！”她们同时喊道。
“Sorry you didn’t win.”
“很遗憾，你没有赢得比赛。”
That was for the golf tournament.
那是为高尔夫球锦标赛而举办的。
She had lost in the finals the week before.
前一周，她已经输掉了决赛。
“You don’t know who we are,” said one of the girls in yellow, “but we met you here about a month ago.”
“你们不知道我们是谁，”其中一个穿黄衣服的女孩说道，“不过我们大约一个月前在这里遇见了你。”
“You’ve dyed your hair since then,” remarked Jordan, and I started, but the girls had moved casually on
“从那以后，你把头发染成了那种颜色，”乔丹说道。我刚要开口，那些女孩们却已经漫不经心地继续走开了。
and her remark was addressed to the premature moon, produced like the supper, no doubt, out of a caterer’s basket.
她的那句话是对那颗过早出现的月亮说的，毫无疑问，那颗月亮就像晚餐一样，是从某个供应商的篮子里被拿出来的。
With Jordan’s slender golden arm resting in mine, we descended the steps and sauntered about the garden.
乔丹那纤细而金色的手臂搭在我的手臂上，我们沿着台阶往下走，然后悠闲地漫步在花园里。
A tray of cocktails floated at us through the twilight, and we sat down at a table with the two girls in yellow
在昏暗的灯光下，一托盘鸡尾酒飘浮在我们面前。我们坐在桌子旁，旁边还有两个女孩，她们都穿着黄色的衣服。
and three men, each one introduced to us as Mr. Mumble.
还有三个男人，他们都被介绍为我们是“Mumble先生”。
“Do you come to these parties often?” inquired Jordan of the girl beside her.
“你经常来参加这些聚会吗？”乔丹问道旁边的女孩。
“The last one was the one I met you at,” answered the girl, in an alert confident voice.
“最后一个，就是我在那里遇见你的那个，”女孩用一种自信而活泼的声音回答道。
She turned to her companion: “Wasn’t it for you, Lucille?”
她转向她的同伴：“难道不是为了你，露西尔吗？”
It was for Lucille, too.
那也是为了露西尔。
“I like to come,” Lucille said.
“我喜欢来这里，”露西尔说道。
“I never care what I do, so I always have a good time. When I was here last I tore my gown on a chair,
“我从来不在乎自己做什么事情，所以总是能玩得开心。上次我在这里时，把连衣裙撕在了椅子上。”
and he asked me my name and address—inside of a week I got a package from Croirier’s with a new evening gown in it.”
他问我名字和地址——一周后，我收到了来自Croirier的包裹，里面装着一件新买的晚礼服。
“Did you keep it?” asked Jordan.
“你留着它了吗？”乔丹问道。
“Sure I did. I was going to wear it tonight, but it was too big in the bust
“当然，我确实戴过了。我本来打算今晚再戴它，但它在胸部处太大了。”
and had to be altered. It was gas blue with lavender beads. Two hundred and sixty-five dollars.”
“而且还需要进行改造。颜色是气体蓝色，还配有一些淡紫色的小珠子。价格是265美元。”
“There’s something funny about a fellow that’ll do a thing like that,” said the other girl eagerly.
“那个家伙做那种事的样子真有趣，”另一个女孩急切地说。
“He doesn’t want any trouble with anybody.”
“他不想与任何人发生任何麻烦。”
“Who doesn’t?”
“谁不会呢？”
I inquired.
我询问了一下。
“Gatsby. Somebody told me—”
“盖茨比。有人告诉我——”
The two girls and Jordan leaned together confidentially.
那两个女孩和乔丹紧紧相依，气氛十分亲密。
“Somebody told me they thought he killed a man once.”
“有人告诉我，他们认为他曾杀过一个人。”
A thrill passed over all of us.
我们所有人都感到一阵激动的情绪在心中涌动。
The three Mr. Mumbles bent forward and listened eagerly.
那三个叫“莫布姆斯先生”的人纷纷前倾身子，全神贯注地聆听着。
“I don’t think it’s so much that,” argued Lucille sceptically; “It’s more that he was a German spy during the war.”
“我不认为有那么大的差别，”露西尔怀疑地反驳道；“更重要的是，他在战争期间是一名德国间谍。”
One of the men nodded in confirmation.
其中一个人点了点头表示同意。
“I heard that from a man who knew all about him, grew up with him in Germany,” he assured us positively.
“我是从一个非常了解他的人那里听到的，他是在德国长大的，和他是一起长大的，”他肯定地告诉我们。
“Oh, no,” said the first girl, “it couldn’t be that, because he was in the American army during the war.”
“哦，不，”第一个女孩说，“不可能那样，因为他在战争期间都在美国军队里服役呢。”
As our credulity switched back to her she leaned forward with enthusiasm.
当我们的信任重新回到她身上时，她便热情地向前倾身。
“You look at him sometimes when he thinks nobody’s looking at him. I’ll bet he killed a man.”
“你有时会看着他，当他以为没人注意的时候。我敢打赌，他肯定杀过一个人。”
She narrowed her eyes and shivered.
她眯起眼睛，身体微微颤抖。
Lucille shivered.
露西尔颤抖着。
We all turned and looked around for Gatsby.
我们都转过身来，四处寻找盖茨比的身影。
It was testimony to the romantic speculation he inspired that there were whispers about him from those
这证明了他那种浪漫的幻想——那些人都在谈论他。
who had found little that it was necessary to whisper about in this world.
那些人发现，在这个世界上，没有什么事情是值得大谈特谈的。
The first supper—there would be another one after midnight—was now being served, and Jordan invited me to join her own party,
第一顿晚餐——午夜过后还会再有一顿——正在准备中，乔丹邀请我参加她的聚会。
who were spread around a table on the other side of the garden.
他们围坐在花园另一边的桌子上。
There were three married couples and Jordan’s escort, a persistent undergraduate given to violent innuendo,
有三对已婚夫妇，还有乔丹的同伴——一个喜欢用暴力方式暗示的、执着的大学学生。
and obviously under the impression that sooner or later Jordan was going to yield him up her person to a greater or lesser degree.
显然，他们以为迟早乔丹会或多或少地交出她的身体给他。
Instead of rambling, this party had preserved a dignified homogeneity,
与冗长的描述相比，这次聚会保持了一种庄重的统一性，
and assumed to itself the function of representing the staid nobility of the countryside—
并且自诩为代表着乡村中那些稳重而高尚的贵族阶层——
East Egg condescending to West Egg and carefully on guard against its spectroscopic gaiety.
东卵对西卵表现出傲慢的态度，并且小心翼翼地避免与西卵那种浮夸的、不恰当的举止打交道。
“Let’s get out,” whispered Jordan, after a somehow wasteful and inappropriate half-hour; “this is much too polite for me.”
“我们还是离开吧，”乔丹在半小时后低声说道，那半个小时实在浪费又不合时宜；“对我来说，这种礼貌实在太过头了。”
We got up, and she explained that we were going to find the host:
我们起身后，她解释说，我们要去找到那个主人。
I had never met him, she said, and it was making me uneasy.
她说，我从未见过他，这让我感到不安。
The undergraduate nodded in a cynical, melancholy way.
那位大学生以一种愤世嫉俗、忧郁的语气点了点头。
The bar, where we glanced first, was crowded, but Gatsby was not there.
我们先扫视过的那家酒吧虽然人很多，但盖茨比并不在那里。
She couldn’t find him from the top of the steps, and he wasn’t on the veranda.
她站在台阶顶上没看见他，门廊上也没有他的影子。
On a chance we tried an important-looking door, and walked into a high Gothic library,
偶然间，我们尝试推开一扇看起来很重要的门，然后走进了一个高大的哥特式图书馆里。
panelled with carved English oak, and probably transported complete from some ruin overseas.
该书架由雕刻精美的英国橡木制成，很可能是从海外某处废墟中运来的。
A stout, middle-aged man, with enormous owl-eyed spectacles, was sitting somewhat drunk on the edge of a great table,
一位身材魁梧的中年男子，戴着一副巨大的猫头鹰式眼镜，醉醺醺地坐在一张大桌子的边缘。
staring with unsteady concentration at the shelves of books.
他目不转睛地盯着书架上的书籍，注意力有些不稳定。
As we entered he wheeled excitedly around and examined Jordan from head to foot.
当我们走进去时，他兴奋地转过身来，仔细打量着乔丹的全身。
“What do you think?” he demanded impetuously.
“你怎么看？”他急切地问道。
“About what?”
“什么事？”
He waved his hand toward the bookshelves.
他朝书架方向挥了挥手。
“About that. As a matter of fact you needn’t bother to ascertain. I ascertained. They’re real.”
“关于那个……其实你不必费心去确认。我已经确认过了，那些都是真的。”
“The books?”
“那些书？”
He nodded.
他点了点头。
“Absolutely real—have pages and everything. I thought they’d be a nice durable cardboard. Matter of fact, they’re absolutely real. Pages and—Here! Lemme show you.”
“绝对真实——有页码之类的细节。我原以为它们会是质地不错的硬纸板制成的。事实上，它们确实非常真实。页码……来吧！让我给你们看看。”
Taking our scepticism for granted, he rushed to the bookcases and returned with Volume One of the Stoddard Lectures.
他忽视了我们的怀疑态度，急忙走到书架旁，拿出了《斯托达德讲座》的第一卷。
“See!” he cried triumphantly.
“看！”他得意地喊道。
“It’s a bona-fide piece of printed matter. It fooled me. This fella’s a regular Belasco. It’s a triumph. What thoroughness! What realism! Knew when to stop,
“是正儿八经印出来的书！我都给骗了。这家伙简直是个贝拉斯科，太成功了！多周到，多逼真！又知道在哪儿收手，
too—didn’t cut the pages. But what do you want? What do you expect?”
书页都没裁开。不过，你还想怎样？还指望什么？”
He snatched the book from me and replaced it hastily on its shelf,
他从我手里一把夺过书，急忙放回架上，
muttering that if one brick was removed the whole library was liable to collapse.
嘴里咕哝着，抽走一块砖头，整个图书室怕就要塌了。
“Who brought you?” he demanded.
“是谁把你带来的？”他问道。
“Or did you just come? I was brought. Most people were brought.”
“或者，你只是被带过来的？大多数人都是被带过来的。”
Jordan looked at him alertly, cheerfully, without answering.
乔丹用一种警觉而愉悦的眼神看着他，但没有回答。
“I was brought by a woman named Roosevelt,” he continued.
“有个人带着我，她的名字叫罗斯福，”他继续说道。
“Mrs. Claud Roosevelt. Do you know her? I met her somewhere last night. I’ve been drunk for about a week now,
“克劳德·罗斯福夫人。您认识她吗？昨晚我在某个地方遇见了她。我已经喝醉大约一周了。”
and I thought it might sober me up to sit in a library.”
“我觉得，坐在图书馆里或许能让我清醒一些。”
“Has it?”
“真的吗？”
“A little bit, I think. I can’t tell yet. I’ve only been here an hour. Did I tell you about the books? They’re real. They’re—”
“我想，应该有一点吧。我还无法确定。我在这里才一个小时而已。我之前有没有告诉过你那些书的事情呢？那些书是真实的，真的……”
“You told us.”
“你告诉我们的。”
We shook hands with him gravely and went back outdoors.
我们严肃地与他握手，然后回到了户外。
There was dancing now on the canvas in the garden; old men pushing young girls backward in eternal graceless circles,
此时，花园里的画布上正有舞者翩翩起舞；那些老人将年轻女孩们推到一边，他们以一种毫无美感的方式，在角落里旋转着……
superior couples holding each other tortuously, fashionably, and keeping in the corners—
那些关系亲密的伴侣相互扶持着，以优雅的姿态站在角落里——
and a great number of single girls dancing individually or relieving the orchestra for a moment of the burden of the banjo or the traps.
还有许多单身女孩在单独跳舞，或者暂时让管弦乐队不必再承担班卓琴或陷阱乐器的负担。
By midnight the hilarity had increased.
到了午夜时分，这种热闹的景象愈发激烈了。
A celebrated tenor had sung in Italian, and a notorious contralto had sung in jazz,
一位著名的男高音歌手用意大利语演唱，而一位著名的女低音歌手则用法语演唱。
and between the numbers people were doing “stunts” all over the garden, while happy, vacuous bursts of laughter rose toward the summer sky.
在花园里，人们纷纷表演着各种“特技动作”，而欢快的笑声则升腾至夏日的天空。
A pair of stage twins, who turned out to be the girls in yellow,
一对舞台双胞胎，结果原来就是那个穿着黄色衣服的女孩们。
did a baby act in costume, and champagne was served in glasses bigger than finger-bowls.
一个婴儿穿着戏服表演，而香槟则被盛在比手指碗还大的杯子里。
The moon had risen higher, and floating in the Sound was a triangle of silver scales,
月亮升得更高了，海峡上浮着一片三角形的银色鳞光，
trembling a little to the stiff, tinny drip of the banjoes on the lawn.
草坪上的班卓琴铮铮地响着，一声一声生硬而单薄，那片银光也跟着微微颤动。
I was still with Jordan Baker.
我还和乔丹·贝克在一起。
We were sitting at a table with a man of about my age
和我们同桌的是个年纪跟我相仿的男人，
and a rowdy little girl, who gave way upon the slightest provocation to uncontrollable laughter.
还有一个闹腾的小姑娘，一有点由头就笑得收不住。
I was enjoying myself now.
这会儿我已经玩得挺高兴了。
I had taken two finger-bowls of champagne, and the scene had changed before my eyes into something significant, elemental, and profound.
两钵香槟下肚，眼前的景象就变了，仿佛有了某种深意，既原始又深邃。
At a lull in the entertainment the man looked at me and smiled.
趁着表演的空当，那人看了看我，露出微笑。
“Your face is familiar,” he said politely.
“您看着有点面熟。”他客气地说。
“Weren’t you in the First Division during the war?”
“打仗那会儿，你不是在第一师吗？”
“Why yes. I was in the Twenty-eighth Infantry.”
“可不是嘛。我在第二十八步兵团。”
“I was in the Sixteenth until June nineteen-eighteen. I knew I’d seen you somewhere before.”
“我在第十六团，一直待到一九一八年六月。我就知道我在哪儿见过您。”
We talked for a moment about some wet, grey little villages in France.
我们聊了几句，说起法国那几个湿漉漉、灰蒙蒙的小村子。
Evidently he lived in this vicinity, for he told me
他显然就住在附近，因为他告诉我，
that he had just bought a hydroplane, and was going to try it out in the morning.
他刚买了一架水上飞机，打算早上去试飞。
“Want to go with me, old sport? Just near the shore along the Sound.”
“要一起去吗，老兄？就在海峡里贴着岸边飞一段。”
“What time?”
“几点？”
“Any time that suits you best.”
“你什么时候最方便，就什么时候。”
It was on the tip of my tongue to ask his name when Jordan looked around and smiled.
我正要问他贵姓，乔丹转过头来笑了。
“Having a gay time now?” she inquired.
“现在玩得开心了吧？”她问。
“Much better.”
“好多了。”
I turned again to my new acquaintance.
我又转向这位新交的朋友。
“This is an unusual party for me. I haven’t even seen the host. I live over there—”
“这场宴会对我来说可真特别。我连主人都没见过。我就住在那边——”
I waved my hand at the invisible hedge in the distance, “and this man Gatsby sent over his chauffeur with an invitation.”
我朝远处那道已看不见的树篱挥挥手，“是这位盖茨比先生派司机给我送来了请帖。”
For a moment he looked at me as if he failed to understand.
他望了我一会儿，仿佛没听懂我的话。
“I’m Gatsby,” he said suddenly.
“我就是盖茨比。”他忽然说。
“What!”
“什么！”
I exclaimed.
我脱口而出。
“Oh, I beg your pardon.”
“噢，真对不住。”
“I thought you knew, old sport. I’m afraid I’m not a very good host.”
“我以为你知道呢，老兄。看来我这个主人当得不太称职。”
He smiled understandingly—much more than understandingly.
他会心一笑。说是会心，还远远不够。
It was one of those rare smiles with a quality of eternal reassurance in it, that you may come across four or five times in life.
那样的笑容十分罕见，带着一种仿佛永远都能让人安心的力量，一辈子大约也就能遇上四五回。
It faced—or seemed to face—the whole eternal world for an instant, and then concentrated on you with an irresistible prejudice in your favour.
有一刹那，它似乎面对着整个亘古的世界，旋即又专注于你，带着一种让人无法抗拒的偏爱，一心向着你。
It understood you just so far as you wanted to be understood,
你希望被了解多少，它就恰好了解你多少；
believed in you as you would like to believe in yourself, and assured you
你多希望自己能相信自己，它就那样相信你，还让你确信，
that it had precisely the impression of you that, at your best, you hoped to convey.
你留给它的印象，恰好是你在最好的时候希望留给别人的那个样子。
Precisely at that point it vanished—and I was looking at an elegant young roughneck,
偏在这时候，那笑容消失了。我眼前只剩一个衣着讲究、略带几分粗野的年轻人，
a year or two over thirty, whose elaborate formality of speech just missed being absurd.
三十一二岁，说起话来刻意讲究礼数，差一点就显得可笑。
Some time before he introduced himself I’d got a strong impression that he was picking his words with care.
早在他自报姓名之前，我就清楚地感觉到，他每句话都经过仔细斟酌。
Almost at the moment when Mr. Gatsby identified himself a butler hurried toward him with the information that Chicago was calling him on the wire.
盖茨比先生刚表明身份，管家就匆匆赶过来，告诉他芝加哥有他的电话。
He excused himself with a small bow that included each of us in turn.
他朝我们一一微微欠身，请我们原谅他失陪。
“If you want anything just ask for it, old sport,” he urged me.
“需要什么只管开口，老兄。”他叮嘱我。
“Excuse me. I will rejoin you later.”
“失陪了。一会儿我再来陪你们。”
When he was gone I turned immediately to Jordan—constrained to assure her of my surprise.
他一走，我立刻转向乔丹，急于让她相信我当真吃了一惊。
I had expected that Mr. Gatsby would be a florid and corpulent person in his middle years.
我原以为盖茨比先生会是个红光满面、大腹便便的中年人。
“Who is he?”
“他究竟是什么人？”
I demanded.
我追问道。
“Do you know?”
“你知道吗？”
“He’s just a man named Gatsby.”
“他就是个叫盖茨比的人呗。”
“Where is he from, I mean? And what does he do?”
“我是问他是哪儿人，做什么的？”
“Now you’re started on the subject,” she answered with a wan smile.
“这下你也问起这个来了。”她淡淡一笑，答道。
“Well, he told me once he was an Oxford man.”
“嗯，他有一回告诉我，他在牛津读过书。”
A dim background started to take shape behind him, but at her next remark it faded away.
他那模糊的身世刚在我眼前现出一点轮廓，她接下来一句话又让它消散了。
“However, I don’t believe it.”
“不过，我可不信。”
“Why not?”
“为什么不信？”
“I don’t know,” she insisted, “I just don’t think he went there.”
“我也说不上来，”她坚持道，“我就是觉得他没去那儿念过书。”
Something in her tone reminded me of the other girl’s “I think he killed a man,” and had the effect of stimulating my curiosity.
她说话的口气让我想起刚才那个姑娘说的“我觉得他杀过人”，倒越发勾起了我的好奇心。
I would have accepted without question the information that Gatsby sprang from the swamps of Louisiana or from the lower East Side of New York.
要说盖茨比出身于路易斯安那的沼泽地，或是纽约的下东区，我都会毫不怀疑地相信。
That was comprehensible.
这些我都能理解。
But young men didn’t—at least in my provincial inexperience I believed they didn’t—drift coolly out of nowhere and buy a palace on Long Island Sound.
可一个年轻人怎么会从不知什么地方悠悠然冒出来，就在长岛海峡边上买一座宫殿呢？至少在我这个没见过世面的外乡人看来，这样的事绝无可能。
“Anyhow, he gives large parties,” said Jordan, changing the subject with an urban distaste for the concrete.
“反正，他办的宴会场面很大。”乔丹换了个话题，带着城里人那种不爱把话说实在的习气。
“And I like large parties. They’re so intimate. At small parties there isn’t any privacy.”
“我就喜欢人多的宴会，多亲密。小派对上反而一点儿隐私都没有。”
There was the boom of a bass drum, and the voice of the orchestra leader rang out suddenly above the echolalia of the garden.
大鼓咚地一响，乐队指挥的声音陡然压过了花园里此起彼应的喧闹。
“Ladies and gentlemen,” he cried.
“女士们，先生们！”他高声喊道。
“At the request of Mr. Gatsby we are going to play for you Mr. Vladimir Tostoff’s latest work,
“应盖茨比先生之请，我们将为各位演奏弗拉基米尔·托斯托夫先生的最新作品。
which attracted so much attention at Carnegie Hall last May. If you read the papers you know there was a big sensation.”
今年五月，这部作品在卡内基音乐厅引起了广泛关注。读报的诸位都知道，当时可是轰动一时啊。”
He smiled with jovial condescension, and added: “Some sensation!”
他带着一副俯就众人的神气，和和气气地笑了笑，又添了一句：“可不是一般的轰动！”
Whereupon everybody laughed.
于是大伙儿都笑了。
“The piece is known,” he concluded lustily, “as ‘Vladimir Tostoff’s Jazz History of the World!’ ”
“这首曲子，”他最后使足了嗓门宣布，“就叫《弗拉基米尔·托斯托夫的爵士世界史》！”
The nature of Mr. Tostoff’s composition eluded me, because just as it began my eyes fell on Gatsby,
托斯托夫先生的曲子究竟是怎样的，我没听进去，因为乐声刚起，我就看见了盖茨比。
standing alone on the marble steps and looking from one group to another with approving eyes.
他独自站在大理石台阶上，目光从这一群人移向那一群人，眼里尽是赞许。
His tanned skin was drawn attractively tight on his face and his short hair looked as though it were trimmed every day.
他晒成褐色的面庞紧致好看，一头短发像是天天都修剪。
I could see nothing sinister about him.
我从他身上看不出一点阴险的样子。
I wondered if the fact that he was not drinking helped to set him off from his guests,
我暗想，他之所以在宾客间显得格外不同，会不会有几分是因为他滴酒不沾？
for it seemed to me that he grew more correct as the fraternal hilarity increased.
在我看来，众人越是亲亲热热地放声取乐，他的举止就越发端正起来。
When the “Jazz History of the World” was over, girls were putting their heads on men’s shoulders in a puppyish,
等《爵士乐世界史》演奏完，姑娘们正把脑袋靠在男人肩上，
convivial way, girls were swooning backward playfully into men’s arms, even into groups, knowing
像小狗一样亲昵嬉闹。有的闹着玩，软绵绵地往男人怀里倒，甚至往一群人身上倒，
that someone would arrest their falls—but no one swooned backward on Gatsby,
反正知道总有人接住她们。可没有一个姑娘往盖茨比身上倒，
and no French bob touched Gatsby’s shoulder, and no singing quartets were formed with Gatsby’s head for one link.
没有一头法式短发碰过他的肩，凑在一起唱四重唱的四颗脑袋里，也从来没有他那一颗。
“I beg your pardon.”
“请原谅。”
Gatsby’s butler was suddenly standing beside us.
盖茨比的管家突然出现在我们身边。
“Miss Baker?” he inquired.
“贝克小姐？”他问道。
“I beg your pardon, but Mr. Gatsby would like to speak to you alone.”
“请原谅，但盖茨比先生希望单独与您交谈。”
“With me?” she exclaimed in surprise.
“和我在一起？”她惊讶地叫道。
“Yes, madame.”
“是的，夫人。”
She got up slowly, raising her eyebrows at me in astonishment, and followed the butler toward the house.
她缓缓起身，惊讶地挑起眉毛，然后跟随男仆走向房子。
I noticed that she wore her evening-dress, all her dresses, like sports clothes—there was a jauntiness about her movements
我注意到，她穿着晚礼服，所有的连衣裙都像运动服一样，她的动作显得很活泼。
as if she had first learned to walk upon golf courses on clean, crisp mornings.
仿佛她最初是在那些干净、清爽的早晨，在高尔夫球场上学走路的姿势一样。
I was alone and it was almost two.
当时我独自一人，时间已经接近两点了。
For some time confused and intriguing sounds had issued from a long, many-windowed room which overhung the terrace.
在一段时间里，从那个有众多窗户的宽敞房间里传出了一些令人困惑且引人入胜的声音，这个房间俯临着露台。
Eluding Jordan’s undergraduate, who was now engaged in an obstetrical conversation with two chorus girls, and who implored me to join him, I went inside.
我躲开了乔丹，他当时正和两个女合唱团成员进行着关于产科的谈话，并恳请我加入他们。我便走了进去。
The large room was full of people.
那间宽敞的房间里挤满了人。
One of the girls in yellow was playing the piano, and beside her stood a tall, red-haired young lady from a famous chorus, engaged in song.
其中一个穿着黄色衣服的女孩正在弹奏钢琴，而她的旁边站着一个高个子、红发的小姐，她来自一个著名的合唱团，也在演唱歌曲。
She had drunk a quantity of champagne, and during the course of her song she had decided,
她喝了很多香槟，在唱歌的过程中，她意识到，
ineptly, that everything was very, very sad—she was not only singing, she was weeping too.
不恰当地说，一切看起来都极其悲伤——她不仅在唱歌，还在哭泣。
Whenever there was a pause in the song she filled it with gasping, broken sobs, and then took up the lyric again in a quavering soprano.
每当歌曲中出现停顿时，她就会用断断续续的呜咽声来填补这个停顿，然后以颤抖的女高音再次演唱那句歌词。
The tears coursed down her cheeks—not freely, however, for when they came into contact with her heavily beaded eyelashes they assumed an inky colour,
泪水顺着她的脸颊流下——不过并不是自由地流淌，因为当这些泪水接触到她那浓密的眼线时，它们便变成了一种墨黑的色彩。
and pursued the rest of their way in slow black rivulets.
他们继续前行，身后的道路上布满了黑色的细流。
A humorous suggestion was made that she sing the notes on her face,
有人提出了一个幽默的建议，即她可以在脸上唱出那些音符。
whereupon she threw up her hands, sank into a chair, and went off into a deep vinous sleep.
于是，她举起双手，坐进椅子里，陷入了深深的沉睡。
“She had a fight with a man who says he’s her husband,” explained a girl at my elbow.
“她和一个自称是她丈夫的男人发生了争执，”站在我旁边的女孩解释道。
I looked around.
我环顾了一下四周。
Most of the remaining women were now having fights with men said to be their husbands.
剩下的女性中，大多数都正在与那些被她们称为丈夫的男人争吵。
Even Jordan’s party, the quartet from East Egg, were rent asunder by dissension.
就连乔丹所在的那个小团体，也就是来自东卵的四人组，也因为分歧而分裂了。
One of the men was talking with curious intensity to a young actress, and his wife,
其中有一个男人正以一种好奇而激烈的方式与一位年轻女演员交谈，而他的妻子则在一旁。
after attempting to laugh at the situation in a dignified and indifferent way, broke down entirely
在试图以一种庄重而冷漠的态度来嘲笑这一幕之后，她彻底崩溃了。
and resorted to flank attacks—at intervals she appeared suddenly at his side like an angry diamond, and hissed: “You promised!” into his ear.
她会不时突然出现在他身边，就像一颗愤怒的钻石，低声对他说：“你答应过的！”
The reluctance to go home was not confined to wayward men.
不愿回家的人并不只是那些行为不端的人。
The hall was at present occupied by two deplorably sober men and their highly indignant wives.
大厅里现在坐着两个行为极其克制的男人，以及他们那些非常愤怒的妻子们。
The wives were sympathizing with each other in slightly raised voices.
那些妻子们用略带沙哑的嗓音互相倾诉着彼此的感受。
“Whenever he sees I’m having a good time he wants to go home.”
“每当他看到我玩得开心时，他就会想要回家。”
“Never heard anything so selfish in my life.”
“我这辈子从未听说过如此自私的行为。”
“We’re always the first ones to leave.”
“我们总是第一个离开的人。”
“So are we.”
“我们也是。”
“Well, we’re almost the last tonight,” said one of the men sheepishly.
“嗯，我们今晚几乎是最后一批了，”其中一个男人羞涩地说。
“The orchestra left half an hour ago.”
“管弦乐队半小时前就离开了。”
In spite of the wives’ agreement that such malevolence was beyond credibility,
尽管那些妻子们一致认为这种恶意行为是不可信的，
the dispute ended in a short struggle, and both wives were lifted, kicking, into the night.
